o: Sweat glands are supplied by cholinergic fibres in sympathetic nerves

Sweat glands are supplied by sympathetic fibres that are cholinergic (sudomotor fibres), an exception to the usual noradrenergic sympathetic pattern.
That is why anticholinergics reduce sweating.
Sweat glands are absent from the lip margins, nipples and glans penis

Sweat glands are absent from the lip margins, nipples and glans penis (also the tympanic membrane, inner prepuce and labia minora), where sebaceous glands are present instead.
These areas are hairless.
Elastic cartilage is found in the epiglottis and auditory tube

Elastic cartilage is found in the epiglottis, the auditory tube and the external ear.
It does not calcify with age.
Hyaline cartilage has a rich blood supply

Last's says only fibrocartilage has a (sparse) blood supply; hyaline and elastic cartilage rely on diffusion.
That is why hyaline cartilage heals poorly.

questions.s: The panniculus carnosus in man is represented by:
o: Platysma and the muscles of the scalp and face

Platysma and the muscles of the scalp and face are the main human remnants of the panniculus carnosus, a sheet of skin muscle.
That is why they are supplied by VII and lie in superficial fascia.
Palmaris brevis

Palmaris brevis is a panniculus carnosus remnant in the hand.
Supplied by the superficial ulnar nerve.
Dartos of the scrotum

Dartos of the scrotum is a panniculus remnant (smooth muscle in this case).
It wrinkles the scrotal skin.
Corrugator cutis ani

Corrugator cutis ani is also listed; Last's adds the subareolar muscle of the nipple.
All four true: E.
The spheno-occipital joint is a primary cartilaginous joint

The spheno-occipital joint is a primary cartilaginous joint (synchondrosis) that ossifies at about 25 years.
A growth site for the skull base.
Intervertebral discs are secondary cartilaginous joints

Intervertebral discs are secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses), typically in the midline.
Like the pubic symphysis and manubriosternal joint.
The first sternochondral joint is a synovial joint

The first sternochondral joint is a primary cartilaginous joint, not synovial.
The second to seventh are synovial.
Articular discs are found in the sternoclavicular and temporomandibular joints

Articular discs are found where joint congruity is low, as in the sternoclavicular and temporomandibular joints (and the menisci of the knee).
They improve fit and distribute load.

questions.s: Hilton's law states that the nerve to a muscle tends to supply:
o: The joint moved by that muscle

Hilton's law: the nerve to a muscle tends to supply the joint that the muscle moves.
So joint pain can refer along the muscle's nerve.
The skin over the joint

It also tends to supply the skin over that joint.
So inflamed joints cause overlying skin tenderness.
The muscle itself

The motor nerve supplies the muscle itself and gives branches to the joint and overlying skin.
That is the essence of the law.
The periosteum deep to the muscle

Supply of the periosteum deep to the muscle is not part of Hilton's law as Last's states it.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
The periosteum does not cover articular surfaces of synovial joints

The articular surfaces of synovial joints are covered by hyaline cartilage, not periosteum.
Periosteum stops at the edge of the articular cartilage.
Subcutaneous periosteum is supplied by the nerve of the overlying skin

Subcutaneous periosteum is supplied by the nerve of the overlying skin; deeper periosteum is supplied by the nerves to nearby muscles.
Periosteum is very pain-sensitive.
Secondary cartilage develops in the head of the mandible and ends of the clavicle

Last's says secondary cartilage develops in certain growing membrane bones, such as the head of the mandible and the ends of the clavicle.
Not related to secondary cartilaginous joints.
Sesamoid bones are constantly present in the tendon of flexor pollicis longus

Last's lists the constant sesamoids as the patella and those in adductor pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis and flexor hallucis brevis, not flexor pollicis longus.
Sesamoids elsewhere are variable.
Superior and inferior venae cavae

The superior and inferior venae cavae have no valves (Last's list).
Pressure changes in the chest are transmitted freely.
Dural venous sinuses and veins of the head and neck

The dural venous sinuses and the veins of the head and neck (including the ophthalmic veins) are valveless.
Allowing spread of facial infection to the cavernous sinus.
Vertebral venous plexuses

The vertebral venous plexuses are valveless, a route for metastatic spread.
Batson's plexus.
Portal vein and its tributaries

The portal vein and its tributaries are valveless (as are hepatic, cardiac, pulmonary and pelvic veins).
So portal hypertension backs up into them. All four true: E.
In the sciatic nerve about 80% of the cross-section is connective tissue

In the sciatic nerve about 80 percent of the cross-section is connective tissue.
That is why it is so tough.
The median nerve has its own artery from the anterior interosseous artery

The median nerve has its own artery from the anterior interosseous artery, and the sciatic from the inferior gluteal.
Large nerves need a dedicated blood supply.
Group C fibres are thinly myelinated preganglionic autonomic fibres

Group B fibres are thinly myelinated preganglionic autonomic fibres. Group C fibres are unmyelinated postganglionic autonomic and slow pain fibres.
A, B, C in decreasing diameter.
About 40% of the fibres in a nerve to a limb muscle are afferent

About 40 percent of the fibres in a nerve to a limb muscle are afferent (from spindles, tendon organs and pain endings).
So "motor" nerves are really mixed.
In the upper half of the body the medial branches reach the skin

In the upper half of the body (down to about T6) the medial branches of the posterior rami reach the skin; below this the lateral branches do.
A Last's principle.
The posterior rami of C7, C8, L4 and L5 have no cutaneous branches

The posterior rami of C7, C8, L4 and L5 (and C1) have no cutaneous branches.
They supply muscle only.
No posterior ramus supplies skin or muscle of a limb

Posterior rami supply only the back muscles and skin; no posterior ramus ever supplies the skin or muscle of a limb.
Limbs are anterior ramus territory.
The cutaneous territory of posterior rami extends to the posterior axillary line

Last's says the cutaneous territory of the posterior rami extends beyond the extensor muscles but does not reach the posterior axillary lines.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Regarding the general plan of body wall innervation:
o: Where a spinal nerve and segmental artery cross, the nerve lies nearer the skin

Where a spinal nerve crosses its segmental artery, the nerve lies nearer the skin.
A general body-wall rule.
The neurovascular plane lies between the middle and innermost muscle layers

In both thorax and abdomen the neurovascular plane lies between the middle and innermost muscle layers.
Internal intercostal/innermost; internal oblique/transversus.
The most caudal root of a limb plexus is distributed entirely to the extensor compartment

The most caudal root of a limb plexus (T1 in the brachial, S3 in the sacral plexus) is distributed entirely to the flexor compartment, showing the richer flexor supply.
Not the extensor compartment.
Limb buds grow out from the lateral strip supplied by lateral branches of anterior rami

Limb buds grow out from the lateral strip supplied by lateral branches of the anterior rami. Their anterior divisions supply flexors and posterior divisions extensors.
This is the basis of the limb plexuses.

questions.s: Muscles with double innervation because of migration between compartments include:
o: Deltoid (axillary and suprascapular)

Deltoid is supplied by the axillary nerve alone, not by the suprascapular nerve.
It is a pure extensor-compartment muscle.
Brachialis (lateral part supplied by the radial nerve)

Last's says the lateral part of brachialis developed in the extensor compartment, so it is supplied by the radial nerve as well as the musculocutaneous.
A dual supply from migration.
Rectus femoris (femoral and obturator)

Rectus femoris is supplied by the femoral nerve only.
The obturator supplies the adductors.
Short head of biceps femoris (common peroneal)

Last's says the short head of biceps femoris migrated from the extensor compartment, so it is supplied by the common peroneal part (unlike the tibial long head).
Answer B: 2 and 4.

questions.s: Concerning Last's rules of segmental innervation of muscles:
o: Muscles sharing a primary action on a joint are supplied by the same segments

Last's rule: muscles sharing a primary action on a joint are supplied by the same segments, usually two.
For example elbow flexors C5/6.
Their opponents are supplied by segments running in numerical sequence with these

Their opponents are supplied by segments running in numerical sequence with these, for example elbow flexion C5/6 and extension C7/8.
So the joint has a block of four segments.
For a more distal joint the spinal centre lies one segment lower

For a joint one segment more distal, the spinal centre lies en bloc one segment lower.
So the wrist is C6/7 and C7/8.
Most upper limb muscles are supplied equally by three segments

Most muscles are supplied equally by two adjacent segments, and some upper limb muscles are predominantly unisegmental.
Not three.
The plantar reflex becomes flexor during the second year

The plantar reflex becomes flexor during the second year; under one year an extensor response is normal.
Corticospinal myelination is incomplete.
Exaggerated tendon reflexes in upper motor neurone lesions reflect release of the fusimotor loop

Exaggerated tendon reflexes in upper motor neurone lesions reflect loss of supraspinal (reticulospinal, vestibulospinal) control, making gamma motor neurones over-excitable (release of the fusimotor loop).
Hence spasticity and clonus.
The abdominal reflexes are lost in upper motor neurone lesions

The abdominal reflexes are lost in upper motor neurone lesions. Beevor's sign indicates weakness of the lower abdominal muscles.
They are superficial cutaneous reflexes.
The anal reflex is a monosynaptic stretch reflex

Last's says the plantar, abdominal, anal and bulbocavernosus reflexes are multisynaptic cutaneous reflexes, not monosynaptic stretch reflexes.
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Derivatives of the first pharyngeal arch include:
o: The malleus and incus

The malleus and incus derive from Meckel's (first arch) cartilage.
So tensor tympani, attached to the malleus, is a first-arch muscle.
The sphenomandibular ligament and lingula

The sphenomandibular ligament and the lingula are first-arch derivatives (the perichondrium of Meckel's cartilage), as is the anterior ligament of the malleus.
A continuous band.
The mandible, formed by ossification of Meckel's cartilage

Last's says the mandible (and maxilla) ossify in membrane around Meckel's cartilage, not by ossification of the cartilage itself.
The cartilage mostly disappears.
Tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini

Tensor tympani and tensor veli palatini are first-arch muscles supplied by the mandibular nerve.
Along with the muscles of mastication, mylohyoid and anterior digastric.

questions.s: Derivatives of the second pharyngeal arch include:
o: Stapes

The stapes is a second-arch cartilage derivative.
Its muscle, stapedius, is supplied by VII.
Styloid process and stylohyoid ligament

The styloid process and stylohyoid ligament are second-arch derivatives; their lengths vary inversely.
A long styloid gives Eagle's syndrome.
Lesser horns and upper body of the hyoid

The lesser horns and upper body of the hyoid are second arch; the greater horns and lower body are third arch.
The hyoid has a dual origin.
Stapedius and posterior belly of digastric

Stapedius and the posterior belly of digastric (with stylohyoid and the facial muscles) are second-arch muscles supplied by the facial nerve.
All four true: E.
The third pouch forms the inferior parathyroid and the thymus

The third pharyngeal pouch forms the inferior parathyroid and the thymus. So the inferior parathyroid descends with the thymus and may be found in the mediastinum.
Ectopic parathyroids follow this route.
The fourth pouch forms the superior parathyroid

The dorsal diverticulum of the fourth pouch becomes the superior parathyroid.
It moves less, staying near the upper thyroid.
The fifth pouch forms the ultimobranchial body, giving the parafollicular cells

The fifth pouch forms the ultimobranchial body, whose cells become the calcitonin-secreting parafollicular (C) cells of the thyroid.
Origin of medullary thyroid carcinoma.
The second pouch forms the auditory tube

The first pouch forms the auditory tube, middle ear and mastoid antrum. The second pouch forms the tonsillar crypts and supratonsillar fossa.
So the second pouch is the tonsil.
The right fourth arch forms the proximal right subclavian artery

The right fourth arch artery forms the proximal right subclavian artery; the left fourth forms the arch of the aorta.
Hence the recurrent nerve relations.
The third arch forms part of the internal carotid artery

The third arch artery forms part of the internal carotid artery (with the common carotid). So the carotid sinus is supplied by IX, the third arch nerve.
A neat developmental link.
The right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the subclavian because the right fifth and dorsal sixth arches disappear

On the right the distal sixth and the fifth arch arteries disappear, so the right recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks round the next artery, the subclavian (fourth arch).
On the left the sixth persists as the ductus.
The second arch artery persists as the stapedial artery in the adult

Last's says the stapedial artery (second arch) does not persist after birth.
A persistent stapedial artery is a rare anomaly. Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.

questions.s: Neural crest cells give rise to:
o: Posterior root ganglia

Neural crest gives rise to the posterior root ganglia, cranial and autonomic ganglia, and Schwann cells.
So most of the peripheral nervous system.
Schwann cells

Schwann cells (and the satellite cells of ganglia) come from neural crest.
Hence neurofibromas are crest-derived tumours.
Chromaffin cells of the suprarenal medulla

The chromaffin cells of the suprarenal medulla are neural crest derivatives.
Phaeochromocytomas arise from them.
Oligodendrocytes

Oligodendrocytes arise from the neural tube (neuroectoderm), not the neural crest.
Central glia are tube-derived.
Paraxial mesoderm forms somites giving sclerotome and myotome

Paraxial mesoderm forms the somites, which give sclerotome (vertebrae and dura) and myotome (body wall muscles), plus dermatome.
Segmentation begins here.
The intermediate cell mass gives the gonads and suprarenal cortex medially

The intermediate cell mass gives the gonads and suprarenal cortex medially and the nephric systems laterally.
The urogenital ridge.
Rathke's pouch arises from ectoderm cranial to the buccopharyngeal membrane

Rathke's pouch arises from ectoderm just cranial to the buccopharyngeal membrane (the roof of the stomodeum) and forms the adenohypophysis.
So the anterior pituitary is ectodermal.
The lateral plate is segmented

Last's says the lateral plate remains unsegmented and gives rise to the limb buds (and body wall).
Answer C: 1, 2 and 3.
Its cranial part forms the pericardium and part of the diaphragm

The septum transversum contributes the fibrous pericardium (its cranial part) and the central part of the diaphragm.
It is a sheet of mesoderm between heart and yolk sac.
It is invaded by cervical myotomes, mainly the fourth

It is invaded by cervical myotomes, mainly the fourth, producing the diaphragmatic muscle.
Hence C3, 4, 5.
Its caudal part is invaded by the developing liver

Its caudal part is invaded by the developing liver, forming the ventral mesogastrium.
The lesser omentum and falciform ligament come from it.
It forms the oesophageal and vena caval openings

Last's says the connective tissue around the oesophageal and vena caval openings comes from the oesophageal mesentery, not the septum transversum.
The dorsal mesentery forms the crura.
The foot is everted

The foot is inverted at birth and gradually everts with growth.
Mild inversion in a newborn is normal.
The spinal cord ends at L1

At birth the spinal cord ends at L3, reaching L1/2 by about 20 years.
Lumbar puncture in neonates is done lower.
The mastoid process is well developed

The mastoid process is absent at birth, leaving the emerging facial nerve unprotected.
It develops after the second year.
The internal ear, middle ear and mastoid antrum are fully developed

The internal ear, middle ear and mastoid antrum are adult-sized at birth; only the mastoid air cells develop later.
Answer D: 4 only.

questions.s: Concerning growth of the skull and face:
o: In the fetus the vertical height of the orbit equals that of the maxilla and mandible together

In the fetus the vertical height of the orbit equals that of the maxilla and mandible together. In the adult it is about a third, because of growth of the maxillary sinus and the alveolar bone.
The face grows down from the skull.
The face elongates rapidly when the permanent teeth erupt from about 6 years

The face elongates rapidly when the permanent teeth erupt, from about 6 years, with growth of the jaws and sinuses.
Facial proportions change markedly.
In the newborn the mental foramen lies near the lower border of the mandible

In the newborn the mental foramen lies near the lower border of the mandible; in the edentulous elderly near the upper border.
In the dentate adult it is midway.
The two halves of the mandible are fused at birth

At birth the two halves of the mandible are separated by fibrous tissue at the symphysis and unite during the first year.
So the newborn mandible has two halves.

questions.s: Bones that ossify in membrane include the:
o: Clavicle

Last's says the clavicle ossifies in membrane (with the skull vault and face).
It is the first bone to ossify.
Bones of the skull vault

The bones of the skull vault ossify in membrane.
The base ossifies in cartilage.
Tuberosity of each terminal phalanx

The tuberosity of each terminal phalanx ossifies in membrane, unlike the rest of the phalanx.
A curious Last's detail.
Squamous and tympanic parts of the temporal bone

The squamous and tympanic parts of the temporal bone ossify in membrane; the petromastoid and styloid parts ossify in cartilage.
All four true: E.
Each vertebra ossifies from three primary centres, a centrum and two halves of the neural arch

Each vertebra ossifies from three primary centres, a centrum and two halves of the neural arch. All are present by about the eighth fetal week.
Secondary centres appear after puberty.
The neurocentral junctions unite by about 7 years

The neurocentral junctions unite by about 7 years; the laminae unite by about 2 years.
So children's spines show these lines.
The costal elements of cervical and lumbar vertebrae have separate primary centres

Last's says the costal elements of cervical and lumbar vertebrae ossify by extension from the neural arch, without separate primary centres. An occasional centre in C7 or L1 gives a cervical or lumbar rib.
Sacral costal elements do have centres.
The tip of the dens has a secondary centre appearing at about 3 years and fusing at 12

The tip of the dens has a secondary centre that appears at about 3 years and fuses at about 12.
Failure gives an os terminale.
It has five primary ossification centres

Last's says the axis has five primary ossification centres: the lower part of the body, two for the halves of the arch and lateral parts, and two for the halves of the dens and upper body.
More than a typical vertebra.
It has no secondary ossification centres

The axis has secondary centres: one for the tip of the dens (appearing at about 3 years and fusing at about 12) and an epiphyseal ring for the lower body (appearing at puberty and fusing at about 25).
So it does have secondary centres.
The dens and lateral parts unite with the body at about 3 years

The dens and lateral parts unite with the body of the axis at about 3 years.
The synchondrosis can mimic a fracture before then.
The dens transmits the weight of the skull to the axis

Last's says the dens bears no weight; the weight of the skull passes through the superior articular facets beside it.
The dens acts as a pivot.
